questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between assurance and insurance.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Both words describe a contract in which a person pays a **premium** to an insurance company, which promises to pay money if a stated event happens. The difference is in the certainty of the event.

**Assurance** (life assurance) covers an event that is **certain to happen**, such as death, although the date is not known. The insured sum is therefore **always paid**, either at death or at the end of a stated term (endowment).

**Insurance** covers an event that **may or may not happen**, such as fire, theft, accident or flood. The company pays only **if the loss occurs**, and the payment is limited to the actual loss (indemnity).

| Point | Assurance | Insurance |
|---|---|---|
| Event covered | Certain (death or reaching a stated age) | Uncertain (fire, theft, accident) |
| Payment | Always paid at some time | Paid only if the loss happens |
| Principle of indemnity | Does not apply (a life has no exact money value) | Applies (the insured gets back only his actual loss) |
| Examples | Whole-life and endowment policies | Fire, motor, burglary, goods-in-transit policies |

questions.enonce_markdown:
Outline any FOUR reasons why insurance is important to businessmen?

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** **Insurance** is a contract by which an insurance company agrees, in return for a premium, to pay the insured for a loss caused by a stated risk. It is important to businessmen for the following reasons.

1. **It gives protection against loss.** If the shop, stock or machines are destroyed by fire, flood or theft, the insurer pays and the business can continue.

2. **It encourages business ventures.** Because the risk is carried by the insurer, the businessman is more willing to start or expand a business.

3. **It makes it easier to obtain credit.** Banks lend more readily to a firm whose assets are insured, since the loan is safer.

4. **It gives peace of mind and avoids sudden large losses.** The firm pays a small known premium instead of risking one large loss that could lead to closure.

(Other correct points: it covers the legal liability of the firm towards customers and workers (public liability, employer's liability); it gives security to employees and so improves their work; it is compulsory in some cases, for example motor third-party insurance; the premium is a known cost that can be planned in the budget; the funds collected are invested and help the economy.)

**Conclusion.** Insurance reduces the risks of trading and helps businesses to survive and grow.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Name and explain any FOUR advantages of a partnership business over a sole trader.

(6 marks)

(ii) Enumerate any FOUR sources of finance to companies.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Advantages of a partnership over a sole trader**

A **partnership** is a business owned by two to twenty persons who agree to run it together and share profits and losses. A **sole trader** is a business owned and run by one person. The partnership has these advantages.

1. **More capital.** Each partner contributes money, so the firm has more capital than one person can provide, and it can expand.
2. **Pooling of skills and ideas.** Partners bring different skills and experience (for example one in buying, one in accounts), so decisions are better and the work is shared.
3. **Sharing of risk and losses.** Losses and debts are shared among the partners, so the burden on one person is lighter.
4. **Continuity and time off.** A partner can rest, fall ill or travel while the others keep the business open. Workers and customers can be served for longer hours.

(Other points: it has more borrowing power, because the lenders can look to several partners; better supervision of staff; partners may be specialised and can handle larger contracts.)

**(ii) Four sources of finance to companies**

1. **Issue of shares (ordinary and preference shares)** to shareholders.
2. **Issue of debentures (bonds)** or long-term borrowing from the public.
3. **Retained (ploughed-back) profits**, that is, profits kept in the business instead of being paid out.
4. **Bank loans and overdrafts** from commercial banks.

(Other correct answers: trade credit from suppliers; leasing and hire purchase of equipment; sale of assets that are no longer needed; government grants and subsidies; loans from development banks.)
